title: The Settling: Drowned Michigan City and What the Lake Kept
body:
# The Settling: Drowned Michigan City and What the Lake Kept

> *Lo! Death has reared himself a throne*
> *In a strange city lying alone*
> *Far down within the dim West,*
> *Where the good and the bad and the worst and the best*
> *Have gone to their eternal rest.*
>
> — Edgar Allan Poe, "The City in the Sea" (1845)

## What It Is

The Settling is not on any GLMZ administrative map. It does not appear in Governance Consortium logistics records, corponation census data, or Emberlace Systems atmospheric surveys. The Maritime Adjudication Board does not acknowledge it because it does not float and therefore is not a vessel; the GLMZ territorial authority does not administer it because there is no infrastructure worth administering and no population generating taxable activity. It occupies the zone between categories where nothing is required to take responsibility for anything.

What it is, physically: the former resort and residential shoreline of Michigan City, Indiana — the old lakefront that Ashgrave Materials needed in order to expand its Zone 11 industrial operations east along the Indiana shore in 2157. Ashgrave required deep-water port access east of their Gary facilities. The engineering solution involved modifying the local shoreline geometry. The modification raised the effective water level against the Michigan City beach district by approximately four meters. The beach houses, the hotels, the old boardwalk infrastructure, the three-story apartment buildings where the casino workers lived — none of it was designed for four additional meters of lake.

Ashgrave compensated the registered residents. The registered residents left. The unregistered residents — the Gray Zone community that occupied the interior blocks, the people for whom there was no compensation mechanism because they did not legally exist — had nowhere to go and were not officially present when the water came in.

The water came in.

## What Remains

On a clear day, standing on the Zone 11 industrial shoreline east of Ashgrave's territorial boundary, you can see them: the upper floors of the Michigan City beach district rising above the lake surface. The old resort hotels still show their upper stories above the waterline. A water tower, improbably, stands nearly complete. The billboard superstructures — the frames that once held advertising, stripped of their panels by years of weather before the flooding — rise like the ribs of something that died reaching upward.

The waterline runs through what used to be the third floor of most of the residential buildings. Below the surface, on calm days when the lake is clear, you can see the rest: the lower floors still intact, windows dark, the interior spaces colonized by the particular slow patience of fresh water. The streets are down there. The parked vehicles are down there. The personal property of every unregistered resident who did not have time or means to move it is down there, silted over now, indistinguishable from the substrate.

Bathysphere Networks' data and power infrastructure passes through the Settling. The subsurface corridors that connect Bathysphere's southern Chicago installations to their Zone 11 relay nodes run beneath the drowned streets. When the water is calm at night and the light from Bathysphere's passing infrastructure pulses through the submerged windows, the Settling glows. Not brightly. Not warmly. A bioluminescent suggestion of light moving through buildings that used to have reasons to be lit.

The people who know the Settling call this the bleed. It is not a metaphor they chose for aesthetic reasons. It is simply what the light looks like: a slow exsanguination of color through the gaps in the old architecture, rising and falling with the pulse cycle of Bathysphere's distribution nodes.

## Tone and Character

Michigan City was a resort town before it was anything else. There was an optimism built into its architecture — the wide windows, the balconies facing the lake, the design of every building oriented toward the water as if the water were a gift rather than a boundary. The buildings are still oriented that way. They always will be.

The Settling does not feel dangerous. It feels like something else, something that takes longer to name. The silence is the first thing. Zone 11's industrial corridor is not quiet — the continuous mechanical operation of Ashgrave's synthesis facilities produces a low-frequency vibration that residents of the zone feel in their teeth before they hear it as sound. But the Settling absorbs this. The water absorbs this. The acoustic property of partially submerged structures is different from either land or open water; the Settling is neither, and it sounds like neither. It sounds like the place the sound goes after it is finished.

People come here. Not many, and not for reasons that look good on paper. Grief is one reason. The specific grief of people who had something here and watched it become this — family, property, a community, a life organized around a particular stretch of shore. Some of them were children when it happened and return as adults because the body stores certain losses in geographic coordinates and occasionally requires the confrontation.

Curiosity is another. The Settling is accessible by small boat, and there are Gray Zone communities along the Zone 11 interior shore that know how to reach the submerged streets — how to navigate between the upper-floor windows, how to find the buildings where the interior spaces are still mostly air-filled, where you can float your boat through what used to be a hallway and see the doors still on their hinges and the fixtures still on the walls. This is not tourism in any organized sense. It is something people do instead of accepting that certain things are just gone.

The third category is people who have no other options. The Settling's partially submerged upper floors are, technically, on land — above the waterline, accessible, structurally intact in most cases. They are also technically within Ashgrave Materials' Zone 11 territorial claims. Ashgrave does not enforce this territorial claim on the Settling because there is nothing there worth enforcing for, and sending personnel into a haunted flood zone to remove squatters generates operational costs that exceed any conceivable return.

There are people living in the Settling's above-water floors. The estimate is somewhere between 800 and 2,000, depending on the season — more in the summer, when the upper floors are warm and the fishing is good; fewer in winter, when the lake ice makes access unpredictable and the wind off the water finds every gap in every structure that water has been finding for sixty-odd years. They are the people with no other option, which is the truest thing that can be said about anyone who ends up in a place like this: they calculated every alternative and the Settling was what was left.

They fish the submerged streets. The biomass concentration in the drowned district is actually substantial — the structure provides habitat, and the lake has been producing an ecosystem in the old resort zone for sixty years, indifferent to what it replaced. The fishing is genuinely good. This is the kind of detail that makes the Settling strange rather than simply sad: that something productive and alive is happening in there, that the catastrophe has been metabolized by the lake into something that feeds people, that the bones of Michigan City are providing shelter for something that eats and grows and reproduces with no awareness that it is doing so inside the skeleton of someone's lost life.

## The Casino Fleet's Memory

The Michigan City Compact — the Free Floating Nation descended from the casino vessels that exploited Indiana's maritime law exemption — maintains a formal practice of silence once per year, observed on the anniversary of the 2157 flooding.

They do not call it a memorial. They do not call it anything. The casino floors go quiet. The games stop. The lights dim to navigation minimum. The vessels that are near the Settling in that year orient to face it, across whatever distance of water lies between them. The Compact's founding families included people from the beach district — casino workers who were already on the water when the modification began and therefore survived it differently than those who were not. The practice of silence is for those who were not.

It lasts forty minutes. Then the lights come back up. The games resume.

The Settling does not know about any of this. It is under water.

## What the Water Keeps

The official record of the Michigan City beach district flooding is a single line in Ashgrave Materials' 2157 Annual Sovereign Operations Report: *Zone 11 coastal geometry modification completed on schedule; shoreline access objectives achieved; registered resident relocation assistance disbursed in full.*

The unofficial record is the Settling itself. The lake keeps better records than Ashgrave. The lake keeps everything — it just reorganizes it into sediment over time, compressing the evidence of what was there into layers that a geologist could read and a lawyer could not. Somewhere in the substrate beneath the drowned streets are the objects that people left behind: the things too heavy to carry, the things they expected to retrieve, the things they did not know were important until they were gone. The lake has been filing these away for sixty years.

At the current sedimentation rate, the substrate will have covered the ground-floor windows entirely by approximately 2290. The towers will still be above the waterline then. The upper floors will still be accessible. The bleed will still glow at night when Bathysphere's infrastructure pulses beneath the old streets.

The Settling will still be settling.
